newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Global phone giants line up for Singapore licence.
newsitem.headline: Global phone giants line up for Singapore licence.

text.p: Several of the world's biggest telecommunications companies appeared on Tuesday to be preparing to bid for a licence to operate telephone services in Singapore when the industry is degregulated in April 2000.
Britain's Cable and Wireless (C&W) said it would definitely make a bid and was looking for a suitable local partner or partners for the venture.
British Telecom Plc (BT), AT&T of the United States and Deutsche Telekom are all considering separate bids, industry sources say.

They will have to compete with a joint venture of two Singapore government-owned firms, Singapore Technologies Telemedia (STT) and Singapore Power, which announced on Monday they would apply for a licence by the deadline of March 1, 1997.

Singapore said in September it would allow at least one, and possibly two, new operators to compete directly with the current monopoly telephone company, Singapore Telecom, from April 2000. Foreign firms must have a 51 percent local partner.
Singapore's three million residents represent a tiny market for large foreign telecommunications companies.
But analysts say domestic users would not be the main attraction for an outside bidder.

"Singapore is an Asian hub," said John Chessher, regional telecoms analyst at Schroders. "It offers lots of gateways to the rest of the region. The icing on the cake is the big and growing market serving multi-national companies -- and a lot of them are based in Singapore," he said.
Announcing its bid on Monday, an STT spokeswoman said a substantial investment would be required to install a full network in Singapore.
"Industry estimates say it could cost up to Singapore $1 billion (US$714 million) to roll out the infrastructure if the bid for the licence were successful," she said.
Richard Goswell, C&W's Southeast Asia and Pacific chief executive, told Reuters on Tuesday that that estimate could be "conservative" if a full infrastructure had to be installed.
But the start-up costs would be relatively small for companies wanting a foothold in Asia's booming markets.
"Cable and Wireless wants to diversify away from its dependence on its subsidiary Hong Kong Telecommunications," said Chessher. "They would get much more Asian traffic in Singapore."
He said BT had also made it clear it was looking for a partner in the region and Singapore would be an attractive base.
BT's Asia Pacific spokesman, Martin O'Connor, told Reuters on Tuesday the company was evaluating the situation and had not yet made a decision on a possible bid.

Analysts said Singapore's position as a business centre and its good infrastructure meant telecommunications firms could use it as a base for a range of regional networks such as call-back services, and could route calls from other Asian services through the island.
"The main reason they want to bid is the opportunity to get into a business with significant exposure to international traffic," said Gautam Kapoor, telecoms analyst at ING Barings.
"Singapore has in excess of one billion minutes of traffic per year, in and out, so it is a very attractive market."
